name: Vitamin B6
summary: Vitamin B6 is a group of related compounds that the body turns into pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP), a helper for more than 150 chemical reactions. It is in many everyday foods, and a real shortage is uncommon in people who eat a varied diet. Unlike most water-soluble vitamins, too much B6 from supplements taken for months can damage nerves.
roles: Breaking down and building proteins (amino acids)
Making brain messengers such as serotonin and dopamine
Making haemoglobin, the oxygen carrier in red blood cells
Breaking down homocysteine, an amino acid in the blood

status.note: This app has no marker for vitamin B6 yet. Labs measure it as plasma pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP), the active form; EFSA uses a level of 30 nmol/L as a sign of adequate status in a population. PLP has real limits: it falls with inflammation, low albumin, high alkaline phosphatase, alcohol, pregnancy and older age, so a low result doesn't always mean a shortage. A very high result in someone with nerve symptoms is worth discussing with a doctor, because supplements are the usual cause of high levels.

signs: Cracks at the corners of the mouth and a sore tongue
Anaemia with small red blood cells
Fits (seizures), mainly in babies or with severe deficiency
atRisk: People who drink a lot of alcohol
Older adults (blood PLP levels tend to fall with age)
People with long-term inflammatory conditions, such as rheumatoid arthritis or inflammatory bowel disease
People on long-term levodopa with carbidopa for Parkinson's disease, especially gel infused into the gut
Pregnant and breastfeeding women (needs are a little higher)

signs: Tingling, burning or numbness, usually starting in the feet and hands
Loss of balance and unsteady walking
high.note: Nerve damage (peripheral neuropathy) from B6 supplements is well documented. It was first described in people taking very large amounts (2 g or more a day), but later reports found it at much lower amounts taken for months or years: the higher the amount, the sooner symptoms appeared. In 2023 EFSA lowered its upper limit for adults from 25 mg to 12 mg a day. Symptoms usually improved after the supplements were stopped, but recovery can take months or longer. B6 is added to many multivitamins, B-complex products, and energy or 'nutritional' drinks, so amounts can add up without people noticing. It doesn't come from ordinary food.

examples: Fish such as tuna, salmon and trout
Bananas, avocados and other non-citrus fruit
foodSources.note: B6 is spread across many foods, so most people who eat a varied diet get enough. The amounts of B6 in foods aren't in this app's food table yet.

forms.name: Pyridoxine hydrochloride
forms.note: The usual form in supplements and fortified foods. It is cheap, stable and well absorbed. Most reports of nerve damage involve this form, mainly because it is the most used.

forms.name: Pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP, P5P)
forms.note: The active form, sold as a supplement and sometimes marketed as safer or better absorbed. There is no good evidence that it works better for health outcomes, and EFSA's upper limit applies to all forms of B6.

forms.name: B6 combined with doxylamine
forms.note: A licensed medicine for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy in some countries, prescribed by a doctor. It is a medicine, not a supplement.

upperLimit.note: EFSA's tolerable upper intake level for adults, including pregnancy and breastfeeding, set in 2023 (it was 25 mg before). It covers B6 from all sources and all forms, and is based on the risk of nerve damage from long-term intake. EFSA found it unlikely to be exceeded from food; the people at risk are regular users of supplements with high amounts of B6.

interactions.note: Large amounts of B6 (above about 50 mg a day in reports) can make levodopa work less well. The other way round, long-term levodopa with carbidopa can lower B6 levels, especially when given as a gel into the gut. Talk to the prescriber before using B6 supplements with levodopa.
Isoniazid blocks B6 and can cause nerve damage. Doctors often prescribe B6 alongside it for people at higher risk; this is part of the treatment plan.

B6 is used for pregnancy sickness, sometimes at high amounts for weeks. EFSA's upper limit of 12 mg a day also applies in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Talk to your doctor or midwife before using B6 supplements in pregnancy.

interactions.with: Other supplements and drinks with added B6
interactions.note: Multivitamins, B-complex products, and energy or 'nutritional' drinks often contain B6. When several are used together, the total can pass the upper limit without anyone noticing.

In a trial in people with diabetic kidney disease, a high-dose tablet of B6 with folic acid and B12 led to a faster fall in kidney function and more heart and blood vessel events than placebo. Talk to your doctor before using high-dose B vitamins with kidney disease.

cautions: Tingling, burning or numbness in the hands or feet while using B6 supplements should be discussed with a doctor, and the doctor told about every product that contains B6.
Check labels: B6 is in many combined products, and amounts far above the reference intake are common.
A real B6 shortage on its own is uncommon; a blood test and a doctor can tell whether it is low and why.

commonUses: May support mood and ease low mood or depression.
May ease premenstrual symptoms (PMS) such as low mood and irritability.
May ease nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy (morning sickness).
May support brain function and lower blood homocysteine, an amino acid linked to heart and blood vessel disease.

origin: Vitamin B6 is a group of related water-soluble compounds that the body turns into pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP), a helper for more than 150 chemical reactions. It is found in many everyday foods, including poultry, fish, organ meats, potatoes, pulses, whole grains and non-citrus fruit such as bananas. A real shortage is uncommon in people who eat a varied diet.

Supplement B6 is made industrially by chemical synthesis. The usual form is pyridoxine hydrochloride; pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (P5P) is also sold. It is often added to multivitamins, B-complex products and fortified foods and drinks.
dosage: The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) sets a population reference intake (PRI) of 1.6 mg a day for women and 1.7 mg for men, 1.8 mg in pregnancy and 1.7 mg when breastfeeding. EFSA's tolerable upper intake level (the most that is likely safe every day) is 12 mg a day for adults from all sources, including in pregnancy and breastfeeding. It was lowered from 25 mg in 2023 because of the risk of nerve damage from long-term intake. These are population values, not personal targets.

An amount commonly used in studies and supplements is anywhere from about 10 mg to 100 mg a day; the premenstrual syndrome trials used up to 100 mg a day, well above today's upper limit. This is not a reference intake or a personal recommendation.

When checking a label, look at the form (pyridoxine hydrochloride or pyridoxal 5'-phosphate), the amount in mg, and all the other products that contain B6, such as multivitamins, B-complex tablets and energy drinks, because the total can pass the upper limit unnoticed. EFSA's upper limit applies to every form. Tingling, burning or numbness in the hands or feet should be discussed with a doctor. People who take levodopa or isoniazid, are pregnant, or have kidney disease should check with their doctor first.

foodAmounts.verdict: Partly. B6 is spread across many ordinary foods, so a varied diet can reach the reference intake. The larger amounts used in some studies and supplements are far more than normal food provides. For example, for the EFSA reference intake, women, about 250 g of chicken breast, grilled, no skin, or about 280 g of beef sirloin steak, grilled.
foodAmounts.notChecked: Food values are from the UK food composition table (McCance and Widdowson's CoFID 2021) built into this app, for the food named. Cooked, stored or processed foods and other brands differ. These are amounts eaten, not absorbed.
